THE LETTER IS AI. THE BOOK IS REAL.
Hello Mike,

I was looking at Catfish Calling, and what stood out to me wasn't just how far the Gary Duba story has escalated by Book 3. It was the fact that the three Florida Man books now function as a complete reader journey.

By this point Gary has gone from the chaos of the original Florida Man through Hogzilla and into Catfish Calling,  where the story somehow manages to involve a snapping turtle, a royal  family, Wacky World, a Mekong catfish named Leotis and Krystal's Lucha  Libre ambitions.

That ridiculous escalation is actually part of  what makes the series commercially interesting. A reader doesn't  necessarily have to stop at the individual book. Wolfpack now offers all  three as a complete and unabridged series, creating a natural path from  discovering Gary to reading the entire story.

I also noticed that Florida Man has accumulated more than 600 Goodreads ratings, while Catfish Calling has nearly 150, so there is already a meaningful reader base around the property.

That made me think about something less visible than the books themselves.

If  you maintain any author-controlled website, newsletter, or commercial  email infrastructure separately from your publisher, I would verify that  the physical postal address used in those messages remains accurate and  appropriate for the way the messages are being sent. I would also  separately check SPF, DKIM and DMARC on any domain you personally  control.

Those are mundane technical details, but they become more  consequential when an author has multiple series and a long backlist. A  reader who arrives through Florida Man may eventually discover Biker, Nexus, Badger,  or your other work. Wolfpack currently lists ten Mike Baron titles,  while your broader bibliography extends considerably further.

In  other words, the valuable asset isn't just the mailing list attached to  one book. It is the ability to keep a reader connected as they move from  one property to another.

I thought that was worth flagging  because a catalog with this much history has considerably more reader  infrastructure to protect than a single-book author does.

Warm regards,

Nathan

text:
I asked grok about this because I don’t know who the Sackler’s are. Grok had this to say: 
In September 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James filed court papers saying her office had identified about $1 billion in wire transfers involving the Sackler family, entities they controlled, and financial institutions. Those records came from just one institution; James had subpoenaed dozens more. Some of the money moved through Swiss accounts and other offshore channels.6
The filing highlighted transfers involving Mortimer D.A. Sackler, a former Purdue board member. One example was $64 million sent in 2009 from a previously unknown trust (Purdue Pharma Trust MDAS) through a Swiss-linked account in Guernsey and then to him. Other transfers totaling about $20 million from a Purdue parent company were redirected into shell companies that owned family real estate in Manhattan and the Hamptons. Some activity continued as late as 2018. James argued the pattern suggested an effort to move and obscure wealth as opioid lawsuits piled up. A spokesperson for Mortimer Sackler called the transfers legal, appropriate, and in many cases years old.7
This was one piece of a larger picture. After Purdue’s 2007 guilty plea and $600 million-plus settlement over OxyContin marketing, family-controlled entities continued taking large distributions out of the company. Later government filings alleged that from 2008 onward the Sacklers directed billions out of Purdue into trusts and holding companies, making assets harder for future creditors to reach. The 2019 New York disclosure came days after a tentative nationwide settlement framework and as Purdue prepared to file for bankruptcy that same month.25
The bankruptcy and related litigation lasted years. An early plan that would have given the Sacklers broad protection from future civil suits was rejected by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2024. A revised $7.4 billion settlement took effect on May 1, 2026. Under that deal the Sacklers contribute the large majority of the cash (up to roughly $6.5–7 billion over time), starting with more than $1.5 billion on the effective date, followed by further installments. Purdue itself paid about $900 million up front. The family gave up the company, which was transferred to a new entity (Knoa Pharma) with no Sackler involvement. Parties that do not opt into the settlement can still sue family members. Funds are meant for abatement, treatment, and some individual victim claims, though many personal-injury claimants have received far smaller amounts than earlier estimates or have been excluded by documentation rules.18
The $1 billion figure was never presented as the family’s total wealth or the full amount moved out of Purdue. It was an early snapshot from limited bank records used by New York to argue that more discovery was needed and that then-current settlement offers were too low. Later bankruptcy and DOJ materials described a much larger multi-year pattern of distributions from the company into family trusts.

How much in tax monies from Texas was Morgan Stanley paid to set up shop here?

Grok’s answer:
Morgan Stanley is establishing a major U.S. operational hub in Dallas (temporary space at Fountain Place downtown, then a new ~700,000-square-foot tower in Uptown targeted for around 2031). The project involves a reported $684 million capital investment by the firm and is projected to support more than 3,800 jobs by 2035. 
Direct state payments (Texas Enterprise Fund and related):
Texas offered a performance-based Texas Enterprise Fund grant of $43,849,500 plus a $40,000 Veteran Created Job Bonus. These come from state taxpayer-supported funds and are among the larger TEF awards. Payments are tied to meeting job-creation and investment milestones; the state can seek repayment if targets are missed. 
City of Dallas incentives:
The Dallas City Council approved an economic-development package of up to $18.5 million in grants. This includes funds tied to job creation/relocation, a grant in lieu of a real-property tax abatement, and reimbursement of certain permitting and development fees. The city also granted 90% business-personal-property tax abatements (5 years at the temporary site and 10 years at the new site). Officials estimated the city would forgo about $4.8 million in tax revenue from the abatements. 
Additional state-level sales-and-use-tax refunds through enterprise-zone designations were being pursued (potential amounts cited in the $3.75–5 million range), and Dallas County provided support, though no specific county dollar figure was publicly detailed in the https://t.co/bN4FwCbhKb short, the largest explicit cash grants from Texas public funds total roughly $62.4 million ($43.89 million state + $18.5 million city), plus several million more in estimated forgone local property-tax revenue. These incentives are typical of competitive economic-development deals and are structured as performance-based rather than unrestricted payments.

text:
Inside a concrete prison cell in Nuremberg, Hermann Göring stripped away the grand illusions of warfare. Speaking quietly to an American army psychologist, the former Reichsmarschall offered no apologies and no remorse for the catastrophic destruction of Europe. Stripped of his jewel-encrusted medals, tailored uniforms, and paracodeine addiction, the second-most powerful man in the Third Reich was awaiting his sentence before the International Military Tribunal. Observers expected fanatical dogma or legal evasions. Instead, in an intimate exchange with intelligence officer Gustave Gilbert, Göring delivered a cold, clinical analysis of political power. With brutal nonchalance, the architect of Nazi rearmament explained that ordinary citizens never desire war, yet any government on earth—dictatorship or democracy alike—can effortlessly herd its population onto the battlefield.
The man on the iron cot was a shadow of his former public persona, yet mentally formidable. When captured in Austria in May 1945, Göring was bloated and carrying thousands of narcotic pills. Confined behind the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, prison warden Colonel Burton C. Andrus enforced a strict regimen. Deprived of drugs and placed on standard rations, Göring shed eighty pounds, regaining an oratorical sharpness that frequently outmaneuvered chief American prosecutor Robert H. Jackson. Captain Gustave Gilbert, a German-speaking psychologist holding a doctorate from Columbia University, enjoyed daily access to the defendants' cells to document their psychological profiles. Testing placed Göring’s intelligence quotient at 138, among the highest in the prison. During their quiet evening visits, Gilbert probed the inner mechanics of the regime, finding a prisoner who spoke with unsettling candor.
The decisive exchange occurred on April 18, 1946, during a recess in the proceedings. Gilbert stopped by cell number five to discuss the trial's evidence regarding the outbreak of the war, remarking that ordinary people were unlikely to feel grateful toward leaders who brought them ruins. Göring shrugged in contempt. "Why, of course, the people don't want war," Göring replied. "Why would some poor slob on a farm want to risk his life in a war when the best that he can get out of it is to come back to his farm in one piece?" It was a universal truth across all borders: common people never wanted conflict, whether in Russia, Britain, America, or Germany. But that reluctance was politically irrelevant. In the end, Göring explained, leaders determined national policy, and it was "always a simple matter to drag the people along."
Gilbert pushed back, seeking to defend the moral legitimacy of representative government. In a democracy, the psychologist argued, citizens possessed a constitutional voice through their elected representatives, and in the United States, only Congress held the authority to declare war. Göring brushed the objection aside as naive civics. "Oh, that is all well and good," he answered, "but, voice or no voice, the people can always be brought to the bidding of the leaders. That is easy." The mechanism required neither genius nor complicated persuasion: "All you have to do is tell them they are being attacked and denounce the pacifists for lack of patriotism and exposing the country to danger." He paused to emphasize the universal durability of the technique: "It works the same way in any country."
Göring was not sharing an abstract theory; he was describing the operational blueprint he had lived. In August 1939, to justify invading Poland to a populace that dreaded another war, the regime staged the Gleiwitz incident, faking a border attack by SS men disguised in Polish uniforms. For years, state headlines warned that the Fatherland was encircled by mortal enemies, while Gestapo basements swallowed anyone who questioned the militarist consensus. Yet Göring’s revelation was far more disturbing than a confession of Nazi guilt. By asserting that the exact same manipulation worked within free societies, he argued that representative institutions offered no immunity against manufactured hysteria. To the Nazi leader, political morality was merely an ornament, and public consent was just an engineering problem solved by weaponizing fear.
On October 1, 1946, the tribunal found Hermann Göring guilty on all counts, sentencing him to the gallows. But on the night of October 15, barely two hours before the executioner was scheduled to enter his cell, Göring outmaneuvered his captors by swallowing a smuggled glass vial of potassium cyanide. In 1947, Gilbert published his records in Nuremberg Diary, preserving the prisoner's private reflections for posterity. While the Third Reich collapsed into ruins, Göring’s cynical formula outlived the regime that perfected it. Delivered in the quiet of a concrete cell, his words remained an enduring diagnosis of political vulnerability: a chilling reminder that peace does not collapse through the malice of the many, but through the ease with which leaders convince the fearful that survival demands war.

text:
The December 1914 Birth and Movement of the Lynching-Ultimatum Story

The earliest surviving accounts I have found of the antisemitic lynching-ultimatum story appear in December 1914, hundreds of days after the Leo Frank trial ended in August 1913, and hundreds of miles from Atlanta, Georgia. Leo Frank was convicted on Monday, August 25, 1913. Yet the early published versions I have traced appear in New York and Chicago more than a year later.

Two writers stand near the beginning of this trail. Christopher Powell Connolly, better known as C. P. Connolly, lived from 1863 to 1935. He was a lawyer, former prosecutor, investigator, and writer for Collier’s Weekly. Arthur Burton Rascoe lived from 1892 to 1957. He was a journalist for the Chicago Tribune who later became a well-known editor and literary critic.

Hundreds of Days Later, Hundreds of Miles Away

The geography is worth keeping in mind. The New York Times and Collier’s Weekly were both published in New York City, roughly 864 modern road miles from Atlanta. The Chicago Sunday Tribune was published in Chicago, Illinois, roughly 716 modern road miles from Atlanta.

These modern driving distances are useful for perspective. The alleged events were supposed to have occurred in and around an Atlanta courtroom during the summer of 1913. The first versions I have found appear hundreds of days later in publications hundreds of miles away.

The ownership of these publications is also worth identifying. In 1914, The New York Times was under publisher Adolph S. Ochs, who had purchased the newspaper in 1896. Collier’s Weekly was published by P. F. Collier & Son. After founder Peter F. Collier died in 1909, his son Robert J. Collier took control. The Chicago Tribune was owned through the Tribune Company. Robert R. McCormick and Joseph Medill Patterson became co-publishers in 1914.

Monday, December 14, 1914: The Threat Is Outside the Courthouse

On Monday, December 14, 1914, The New York Times published “Finds Mob Frenzy Convicted Frank,” using material from C. P. Connolly’s investigation for Collier’s Weekly. This appeared 476 days after Frank’s conviction, or 68 weeks later. Put another way, 1 year, 3 months, and 19 days had passed since the jury returned its verdict.

In this version, the alleged antisemitic threat is outside the courtroom among people gathered around the courthouse on verdict day. Connolly claimed people around the courthouse were talking about getting Frank whether he was innocent or guilty. The target was Leo Frank. The location was outside the courthouse. The time was verdict day.

This point needs to remain clear because the December 14 story does not place men inside the courtroom threatening jurors during the presentation of evidence.

Saturday, December 19, 1914: The Threat Moves to a Lawyer’s Telephone

Five days later, on Saturday, December 19, 1914, Collier’s Weekly published Connolly’s article, “The Frank Case.” This appeared 481 days after Frank’s conviction, or 1 year, 3 months, and 24 days later.

Now a related antisemitic threat appears in a completely different setting. Connolly said he was visiting the office of one of Frank’s lawyers when the telephone rang. An unknown caller allegedly threatened the lawyer with hanging if Frank was not hanged.

The location has now changed from the crowd outside the courthouse to a telephone inside a defense lawyer’s office. Connolly did not identify the lawyer, did not identify the caller, and did not give an exact date for the alleged telephone call.

This version also does not place the threat inside Judge Leonard Roan’s courtroom or direct it toward the jurors during Frank’s trial.

Sunday, December 27, 1914: Rascoe Moves the Threat Into the Courtroom

Eight days later, on Sunday, December 27, 1914, Arthur Burton Rascoe published “Will the State of Georgia Hang an Innocent Man?” in the Chicago Sunday Tribune. His article appeared 489 days after Frank’s conviction, or 1 year, 4 months, and 2 days later. It was published in Chicago, roughly 716 modern road miles from Atlanta.

Here the story changes again, and this change is the most important one.

Rascoe places the alleged lynching threat inside the courtroom itself. Men in the courtroom audience are now said to have threatened the jurors during court proceedings, warning them to convict Frank or face violence themselves.

The location has changed again. The target has changed too.

Connolly’s December 14 account describes hostility outside the courthouse aimed at Frank.

Connolly’s December 19 account describes an anonymous telephone threat aimed at one of Frank’s lawyers.

Rascoe’s December 27 account puts threatening men inside the courtroom and aims the threat directly at the jury.

Thirteen Days, Three Different Settings

Now place the three accounts beside one another.

On December 14, The New York Times places the alleged antisemitic hostility outside the courthouse around verdict day.

On December 19, Collier’s Weekly places a related threat over the telephone in the office of one of Frank’s lawyers.

On December 27, the Chicago Sunday Tribune places the threat inside the courtroom itself during court proceedings, with the jurors as the targets.

In only thirteen days, the published story travels from the street outside the courthouse, to a telephone in a law office, and then into the courtroom.

The people being threatened also change. First Frank is the target. Then one of his lawyers is the target. Finally, the jurors become the targets.

The timing changes with it. The December 14 account concerns verdict day. The December 19 telephone story has no exact date. Rascoe’s December 27 version pushes the threat back into the trial itself.

What Changed?

The change is easy to see when the accounts are placed in date order.

The location changes.

The target changes.

The time changes.

The wording changes.

By December 27, the story has reached the form later writers would repeat for generations: men inside Leo Frank’s courtroom threatening the jury over Frank’s fate.

I have found no proof showing Rascoe directly copied Connolly and deliberately rewrote his story. The publication dates do show a clear change in the published accounts during December 1914.

The December 14 New York Times account appeared 476 days after Frank’s conviction.

The December 19 Collier’s Weekly article appeared 481 days after the conviction.

The December 27 Chicago Sunday Tribune article appeared 489 days after the conviction.

The first two were published in New York City, roughly 864 modern road miles from Atlanta. The third appeared in Chicago, roughly 716 modern road miles away.

The Main Point

The earliest versions I have found did not appear in the Atlanta newspapers while Leo Frank was actually on trial during July and August 1913. They appear hundreds of days later and hundreds of miles away.

And when those December 1914 accounts are read in chronological order, the story does not stay in one place.

It begins outside the courthouse.

Five days later, it appears over a telephone in a lawyer’s office.

Eight days after this, it enters the courtroom itself.

Within thirteen days, an alleged antisemitic threat aimed at Frank outside the courthouse had grown into a direct lynching ultimatum supposedly aimed at the jurors inside Leo Frank’s courtroom.

The New York Times
Monday, December 14, 1914
Page 4, Column 3
Finds Mob Frenzy Convicted Frank
“Politics, Prejudice, and Passion” at Heart of Case, Collier’s Investigator Declares.

Facts Point to Innocence

Negro Accuser Obviously Undependable, Mr. Connolly’s Article Shows — Unclaimed $5,000 Reward.

Below will be found a graphic picture of the Frank case. It was prepared for Collier’s Weekly by C. P. Connolly and is the first of two articles dealing with this remarkable case to appear in that periodical. The second article will be printed in the issue of Collier’s for Dec. 26.

The writer, Mr. Connolly, has had long experience as a practicing lawyer and prosecuting attorney, and is well known as an investigator. He represented Collier’s at the trial of Haywood and Pettibone in Idaho, at the trial of the McNamaras in Los Angeles, and in other important cases.

Mr. Connolly spent weeks at Atlanta investigating the Frank case. He points out that he went there with an open mind, without prejudice, and with only one purpose in view, to learn the truth. He finds that Frank did not have a fair trial; that his conviction was the result of popular passion, which demanded a victim, and that all the facts point, not to Frank’s guilt, but to his innocence and to the negro Conley as the murderer.

Stress is laid by Mr. Connolly upon the fact that Frank was convicted “largely on the theory that he was a degenerate.” William J. Burns, after his conviction, offered a reward of $5,000 to any one who would produce evidence of a single immoral act of Frank’s whole life, without producing a claimant; and then the police of Atlanta made the astonishing statement that they had never known that Frank was a degenerate.

Here is Mr. Connolly’s opening article, in part:

Saturday, April 26, 1913, a holiday, Mary Phagan went from her home in Atlanta to the National Pencil Factory at which she worked to get some pay still owing her. She did not return to her home. A search was instituted without success. At 3:30 o’clock the following morning her body was accidentally discovered in the basement of the pencil factory by the night watchman, whose duty it was to make the rounds of the building.

Two men were immediately arrested. One was Frank, who was superintendent of the factory, who admitted having paid the girl her wages in his office at noon on Saturday. The other was Newt Lee, the night watchman, who had discovered the body. Alongside Mary Phagan’s body were found two illiterate notes in pencil, purporting to have been written by the victim, and stating how “the long, tall, black negro” had done it.

The notes were manifestly a clumsy invention of the murderer to divert suspicion. It soon became apparent that the night watchman was not the guilty person. Suspicion fastened on Frank and rapidly intensified. During the next three or four days the police, the newspapers, and practically the entire population of Atlanta came to the conclusion that Frank was the guilty person.

Then a third man, a negro named Jim Conley, who also worked in the factory, but who was not known to have been in the factory at the time of the murder, was accidentally discovered washing a stained shirt. He was arrested and held as a suspect, but suspicion was not seriously directed toward him. The stained shirt was returned to him by the police, and his name was practically eliminated until three weeks later, when it was discovered that he could write. He had previously denied that he could write.

Conley’s Bewildering Stories.

Still later it was discovered and admitted by Conley that he had been in the factory at the time of the murder. When the fact that he could write was pressed upon him he told in succession four different formal stories, each of which was taken down by the police. On the trial he told a fifth different story.

His first story was that he had not been at the factory at all. His second story, in which he still maintained that he was not at the factory on the day of the murder, admitted that he had written one of the notes, but claimed that he had done so at Frank’s dictation some time prior to the murder. Frank had “written the other note,” he said he had no idea at the time what use Frank was to make of the note. He did not admit having written both notes until two months afterward when he was sworn as a witness on the stand.

He finally claimed that he had helped Frank carry the body from the second story of the factory, where Frank had murdered the girl, to the cellar. He gave as his reason for not telling this story at first that Frank had promised to protect him and he was waiting for Frank to make his promise good.

The fastening of the crime on Frank as the result of a public opinion which demanded a victim grew rapidly stronger.

No defendant in a criminal case in Georgia may give testimony under oath in his own behalf; nor is he offered an opportunity either for or against him, but he may make a statement not under oath to the jury. His own lawyers are not allowed to ask him any questions, and the prosecutor never asks any, for he fears the answers of a witness not subject to the penalties of perjury.

When Frank had concluded his four-hour statement to the jury the crowd in the courtroom, though mostly antagonistic to him, was deeply moved. It was one of those moments so rarely experienced of an audience absolutely spellbound. Moisture was in the eyes of some of the jurors.

“The statement,” said one newspaper which all along has been antagonistic to Frank, “carried the ring of truth in every sentence, and scores in the room whose minds hadn’t been made up left the courtroom convinced of the man’s innocence.”

During one of the days of intense excitement in vogue throughout the trial, as Frank was being taken from the courthouse to the jail, the crowd wedged threateningly about the automobile. Sheriff Wheeler Mangum, an outspoken believer in Frank’s innocence, hurriedly told Frank to get under cover behind him.

“I am an old man,” said this brave Confederate veteran, “and you are young. If they ‘get’ you, it will be over my dead body.”

The Ring of Truth.

Frank has been twice sentenced to die, the last time on his birthday. When on that last occasion he was asked if he had anything to say, he made a remarkable statement. As showing its effect even in cold print, United States Senator William E. Borah of Idaho told me, prior to my visit to Atlanta, that it so gripped him at the time that he was half inclined to take a train and go to Atlanta for the purpose of learning more about the case. Speaker Champ Clark summed it in his frequent scrap-book as a rare gem. He declared it one of the most remarkable and convincing statements he had ever read. When Frank had concluded his statement there was hardly a dry eye in the courtroom, according to many witnesses.

Some may say that thousands of men in Europe are being sacrificed in a senseless war, and that, after all, the fate of Frank is no worse than that of others who must suffer in this world of injustice and mistakes.

Under a constitutional amendment adopted in 1906 the Supreme Court of Georgia is not allowed to reverse any capital case where no error of law has been committed in the trial, no matter how weak the evidence may be, and cannot investigate or pass upon the question of guilt or innocence. Two of the Supreme Court Judges were for reversing the case on alleged errors of law, but four voted to sustain the conviction.

An Atmosphere of Riot.

While Frank’s trial was pending and just prior to the jury retiring for deliberation, Judge L. S. Roan, who presided, held a consultation on the bench, and in the presence of the jury, with the Chief of Police of Atlanta, and with the Colonel of the Fifth Georgia Regiment, to decide on the best means of protecting Frank in case of his acquittal by the jury. The Fifth Regiment was kept under arms throughout the night.

Before delivering his charge to the jury, Judge Roan also called the lawyers into another room and advised that neither Frank nor his counsel be present when the verdict of the jury was rendered.

While the prosecuting attorney was making his concluding argument in the case, the newspaper editors of Atlanta joined in a petition to the presiding Judge to adjourn the case over for a day, “because,” as The Atlanta Journal said, “it was known that a verdict of acquittal would cause a riot such as would shock the country and cause Atlanta’s streets to run with innocent blood.”

It was common street talk that if the jury discharged Frank, or dared to disagree, Judge Lynch would take a hand before Frank could reach his home or the jail. “Innocent or guilty, we will get the d— Jew,” was a remark frequently heard in the crowd around the Court House on the day of the verdict. The mob was breathing vengeance in the very face of the Judge and jury.

When the verdict was rendered, street car employes quit their street cars to join the crowds that cheered; women in fashionable groups in Atlanta’s stores and semi-social functions clapped their hands. It was a Roman holiday in Atlanta. The news of the verdict was chalked up on the score board at a baseball game at Piedmont Park, and a wild demonstration of approval ensued in the grandstand and on the bleachers. Hundreds “caterwauled” for an hour in front of the pencil factory of which Frank had been the Superintendent and where the girl had been murdered. Telegrams were also sent congratulating the jury.

The Crowd in a Frenzy.

A veritable honeycomb of humanity spread over the section from Whitehall to Central Avenue, on Hunter Street, and from Alabama to Mitchell on Pryor. Men and women clung to the walls of buildings and stood in doorways. Windows were crowded with women and girls and children. It was as though a street audience had gathered to watch an eventful procession. The shrill orders of the mounted policemen rose over the hum of the crowd.

As the reporters at the telephone shouted the verdict to their offices, the word came through the windows. It was received with a shout. The cry of “guilty” took flight from lip to lip. It traveled like the rattle of musketry. Then came a combined shout that rose to the sky. “Pandemonium reigned. Hats went into the air. Women wept and shouted by turns.”

As Solicitor General Dorsey appeared in the doorway of the Court House, while the crowd reeled its reception of the Frank verdict, three men almost lifted him from his feet. The Solicitor reached no farther than the sidewalk, where the mounted men rode like Cossacks through the swarm. The muscular men swung Mr. Dorsey, the prosecuting attorney, on their shoulders and passed him over the heads of the crowd across the street to his office.

Time and again the crowd in the courtroom clapped their hands and stamped their feet in approval of some act of the prosecutor and laughed aloud at the objections of Frank’s lawyers.

When Frank’s lawyers in the early stages of the trial called the names of several Jewish ladies as character witnesses for Frank, the crowd jeered and laughed.

A Critical Moment.

When Solicitor General Dorsey, the Prosecuting Attorney, was in the middle of his impassioned argument, pointing out how this “fiendish degenerate” took Mary Phagan’s life, he held up the bloody clothes before the jury and, dramatically pointing to them, said: “I ask you to look at them — ask you to look at them.”

In the tense stillness Mary Phagan’s mother uttered a terrifying shriek. The crowd in the courtroom rose as a man to their feet. The hands of numbers of those men went to their pockets. Every Bailiff in the room instantly called out in excited tones: “Order! Order!” It was a critical moment.

This gives only an idea of the scene. As the Prosecutor concluded his fiery address to the jury, he dramatically repeated the words “guilty, guilty, guilty,” while with each “guilty” the bell in a neighboring church simultaneously tolled, and the superstitious crowd regarded it as Providential approval of the words.

There is no more in all the gamut of human passion that has not been sounded in the Frank case. There is not a fabric of civilization which it does not touch somewhere — the press, the courts, the police system, labor and capital, racial prejudice, politics, the hue and cry of the impassioned pack hungering for the blood of their fellow. But for brevity, the heart of the Frank case may be summed up in three words — politics, prejudice and perjury.

Epp’s Fantastic Tale.

Again there were stories, facts, and suspicions that found their way into the newspapers in floods. George Epps, a youth of 15, who claimed to be a chum of Mary Phagan, swore at the Coroner’s inquest, a few days after the tragedy, that he had ridden to town from Bellwood with Mary Phagan on the street car on her way to the factory that Saturday.

He said that on that trip Mary told him of attempts Leo Frank had made to flirt with her, and of apparent advances in which he was daily growing bolder.

“She said she was getting afraid. She wanted me to go to the factory every afternoon in the future and escort her home. She didn’t like the way Mr. Frank was acting toward her.”

These alleged remarks of Mary Phagan were not competent evidence under well-known legal rules.

The motorman and conductor of the car contradicted Epps as to his presence on the car that morning with Mary. They knew her well and said she was alone.

The police gave to the newspapers mysterious hints of telephone operatives who were prepared to swear to certain damaging conversations over the pencil factory’s line on the night of the tragedy. These witnesses never materialized at the trial.

A woman of the underworld came forward with a story of how Frank had repeatedly telephoned her Saturday night between 6:30 and 10 o’clock, begging for a room. She declared that Frank had been a frequent visitor at her house and that since his arrest she had had a secret conference with him in the jail.

Jewish Stranger from the North.

Stories of Frank’s alleged philandering freely inconsistent with the conduct of his whole life filled the air, every one of which was later shown to be false.

Frank was practically a stranger in Atlanta, unknown except to a small circle. He and his wife lived with Mrs. Frank’s parents. Frank was President of the local B’nai B’rith, a charitable and fraternal organization. He was strictly devoted to his business and outside his own circle was little known in Atlanta. He had lived in the city less than five years.

The public from the beginning seemed ready to believe anything about this young Jewish stranger from the North. One slander was multiplied into a hundred, and all were accepted without question in the state of public fanaticism.

Among the suspects was a negro man named Jim Conley who had been arrested on the Thursday succeeding the murder because of the fact that he was seen washing a shirt in the factory. He was a floor sweeper employed on the fourth floor.

Conley lay in jail for three weeks, almost forgotten, while the whirlwind of calumny had been swirling about Frank’s head.

This description was exactly the reverse of Jim Conley’s physical characteristics. The notes described the murderer as a “long, tall, slim, black negro.” Conley is short and stout, with a ginger-cake complexion.

Experts’ Shrewd Conclusions.

One of the first efforts of the police was to locate the author of these notes. In pursuance of this purpose, each of six suspects, among them Frank and Newt Lee, were required to write portions of the notes.

All of the suspects gave specimens of their handwriting without hesitation except Conley, who claimed that he could not write.

A bank teller supposed to be an expert declared that these notes were in the handwriting of Newt Lee, the negro night watchman; another bank official in Atlanta declared they were in the disguised handwriting of Leo Frank. One expert declared that the notes were undoubtedly the spontaneous hand of a negro man, with intent to reflect guilt upon an illiterate negro.

Grand Jury Kept in Dark.

Conley’s presence in the factory was unknown and unsuspected by every one connected with the unravelment of the mystery until May 28, ten days after it was discovered he could write.

During all that time he denied having been at the factory that day, in strong contrast to Frank, who promptly admitted he had seen the little girl at the factory and had paid her off.

Frank was indicted after the police and the Prosecutor knew that Conley had admitted he authored the “murder notes,” but the Grand Jury was not advised of this fact.

Conley had no mission at the factory that day, unless his story, told for the first time at the trial, was true, that he was there at Frank’s direction, fortified with a bottle of cheap whisky, to see that nobody entered the factory during Frank’s dalliances.

At the foot of the stairway was an elevator shaft which led to the still darker cellar or basement, and alongside of this elevator shaft was also a trap door leading to the basement by means of a ladder — the “hole” referred to in one of the “murder notes.”

If my theory of this crime is correct, the negro made the notes in part tell truth, just as he made his main story in part tell truth.

The September 28, 2019 Convention de la Droite was organized by figures around Maréchal, including networks such as L’Incorrect, Audace, and Racines d’Avenir, and explicitly presented itself as constructing an “alternative to progressivism.” Maréchal herself described such initiatives as part of a broader cultural-political “basculement” and invoked Gramscian cultural hegemony. text:
Good news for Americans worried that the health insurance industry lacks a voice in Washington:

@MAHA_Action is finally giving it a platform.

The summit’s “Affordability First” panel features executives from UnitedHealth Group and Elevance Health, alongside the head of AHIP, the health insurance industry’s trade association. 

A senior CMS official will moderate. 
No patient advocate is listed on the panel.

An inspired arrangement. If you want to understand why dinner is so expensive, assemble the restaurant owner, the landlord, and the company that charges you a convenience fee for looking at the menu.

The customer can submit a question through the portal.

There is something beautifully efficient about putting the insurance industry in charge of the affordability conversation. Usually, Americans have to spend forty-five minutes on hold to hear an insurer explain their financial circumstances to them. Here, the explanation comes with stage lighting.

And “Affordability First” is an excellent title. It leaves the essential follow-up question, affordable for whom?The answer is available for a future breakout session.

Remember, this is the political movement whose leading health official, @RobertKennedyJr  declared: “We are ending the corporate capture of public health.”

Apparently, the treatment involves exposure therapy.

Start with a small dose of corporate leadership. Increase gradually until the patient can enter a ballroom full of executives without remembering why they were angry.

Later, the summit offers “Prevention at Scale,” featuring the CEOs of @Ascensionorg , @SutterHealth, and 
@advocatehealth.

Between the two panels, the institutions that finance care and the institutions that deliver it enjoy a substantial opportunity to explain the future. The person trying to figure out whether they can afford an MRI remains an exciting opportunity for stakeholder engagement.

Imagine a different affordability panel. A patient brings a bill. A physician brings the paperwork required to get treatment approved. An insurance executive gets a microphone and has to explain both.

That would be a useful conversation. It might also run over 30 minutes, particularly if someone insisted on answering the question.

Instead, this lineup offers the familiar Washington comfort of discussing people’s problems at a professional distance from the people having them. From the stage, a medical bill can become a challenge involving incentives, innovation, and complex systems. At the kitchen table, it remains a number you cannot pay.

The appeal of an anti-establishment movement is the promise that someone will finally make the powerful uncomfortable. Looking at these panels, the powerful appear to have been accommodated quite thoughtfully.

There is a chair. There is a microphone. There is a moderator to keep things moving.

For everyone who thought making America healthy again might involve making its health care institutions answer to patients, please be patient.

Your revolution is important to us.
Please remain on the line.

Born & raised in Frisco for the most part myself. Here’s a list • Golden Gate Bridge – Walk or bike across, or view it from Crissy Field or Marin Headlands.
• Alcatraz Island – Historic abandoned prison in the middle of the bay (remind them to book tickets weeks in advance).
• Painted Ladies – The famous row of colorful Victorian houses at Alamo Square (seen in the Full House intro).
• Lombard Street – The "crookedest street in the world" with eight sharp hairpin turns and beautiful gardens.
• Coit Tower – Offers 360-degree views of the city and bay, plus historic murals inside.
Waterfront & Dining
• Pier 39 & Fisherman’s Wharf – Famous for the sunbathing sea lions, sourdough bread bowls, and seafood.
• Ferry Building Marketplace – A historic terminal turned into a massive food hall with artisanal local eats and a farmers market.
• Ghirardelli Square – The historic brick chocolate factory, perfect for huge ice cream sundaes.
Neighborhoods & Culture
• Chinatown – The oldest and one of the largest Chinatowns in the U.S. (make sure to walk through the Dragon's Gate and visit the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory).
• The Mission District – Famous for vibrant street murals (Balmy Alley/Clarion Alley) and the best Mission-style burritos.
• Haight-Ashbury – The historic epicenter of the 1960s hippie counterculture movement, now filled with vintage shops.
Parks & Outdoor Spaces
• Golden Gate Park – A massive park home to the Japanese Tea Garden, San Francisco Botanical Garden, and the Conservatory of Flowers.
• Twin Peaks – Two prominent hills near the center of the city offering a breathtaking panoramic view of the entire Bay Area.
• Lands End – A coastal trail offering rugged, scenic views of the ocean and the Golden Gate Bridge, plus the historic Sutro Baths ruins.
Unique San Francisco Experiences
• Ride a Cable Car – Hang off the side of a historic moving landmark, especially on the Powell-Hyde line for great views.
• Museums – Visit the California Academy of Sciences (which has an indoor rainforest) or SFMOMA for modern art.

Gazing into the Mediterranean horizon, Alexandra sought her escape. She had spent a healthy part of the last six weeks frolicking the salty seas—from the beaches of the Portuguese Algarve to those of the Greek Islands—exercising a type of Polynesian ocean worship she had sampled in Hawaii. The waves had been middling, but time in the sun had left her skin nicely bronzed. Haifa provided ideal conditions for bodysurfing. The ankle waders found interest in her antics. Some offered applause, while others gawked as if she were a rumbustious sea creature that kept washing ashore.
--There was one dogged frowner: a thickset woman with golden curls spilling out of her bathing cap, who, if raised in Japan, would have been trained in the art of the Sumo. Now she stood waiting with two police officers, pointing.
--Alexandra was unsure of her offense, awash in a strange land and knowing few of its rules. Her Jantzen swimsuit clung to her lithe frame modestly. Perhaps it struck blasphemously to display wet hair in the ancient Holy Land. She jumped bashful waves that broke close to shore and ducked under the churning lather of those so forceful they collapsed under their weight out to sea. Having the patience to corral the ideal wave proved key, and likely her only chance, short of swimming for Cyprus, to avoid arrest.
